Question: How do you write your non-fiction e-book for Kindle? Do you use Notepad, MS Word, OpenOffice, Google Docs, or another tool before importing it into Kindle Create? Do you use the "native" styles (title, subtitle, etc.) or a customized template?
Answer: When I write, I use Google Docs. The book is not published, in print or in ebook, from a Docs file, though. Instead, after editing, the manuscript is laid out in Adobe InDesign. The InDesign file is sent to the printer as a PDF (well, actually two, one for the cover and one for the interior), then exported as an ePub which is brought into Calibre for fine-tuning and cleanup. How I write: How the book is laid out: How the eBook is laid out: The Google Docs file is exported to Word to be brought into InDesign, but all the Word styles are stripped out and instead the various elements of the book are assigned styles created specifically for that book in InDesign. You can see the Styles palette in the second screenshot. The InDesign styles are set up for both print and ePub, and in particular the “Split Book for ePub” style is used for chapter headers and anything else that must start on a new page, so that the ePub breaks into chapters correctly. (This is something novices frequently fall afoul of; setting up styles with an eye toward how they’ll be used in the ePub, and particularly where the internal ePub files will split, is absolutely crucial.) No professional publishing workflow uses Word files directly, for print or eBook publishing. The manuscript might be given to the publisher in Word format, but the Word file is placed in a page layout app. These days that’s almost always InDesign, though some folks still use QuarkXPress and a tiny handful cling to Frame Maker. (LaTeX markup is occasionally used in niche publishing, like for math textbooks.) This workflow (word processor of some sort, be that Docs or Scrivener or Word or whatever -> InDesign -> eBook editor like Calibre or Sigil) is pretty typical in the publishing industry. Outside of textbooks, it probably accounts for 80% of all the books professionally published.

Question: Should I say "As the launch date for approaches, preparations and procedures are intensifying", "… preparations and procedures are intensive", or some other wording?
Answer: It depends. What is it you’re trying to say? Those two things have slightly different meanings. “Preparations and procedures are intensifying” means preparations and procedures have been going on for an indeterminate amount of time, but are now ramping up—becoming even more intense. “Preparations and procedures are intensive” means that preparations and procedures are currently going on at a high pace, but says nothing about when they started. Perhaps they only just started. “Preparations and procedures are intensive” is okay grammatically, but sounds slightly odd to a native speaker of American English. If you intend to say that the preparations have not been going on for a while and picked up, it might be better to say “intensive preparations and procedures have begun,” or “preparations and procedures are intense.” There are subtle shades of distinction that might not be important; the first suggests the preparations have only just started, while the second doesn’t say anything at all about whether they’ve been going on or they’ve only just begun.

That’s really fast, the equivalent of about Mach 22 at sea level. Question: Why are distorted human faces, with big round eyes and showing teeth or with a strange expression, more frightening than other frightening things?
Answer: This is a surprisingly deep and subtle question, and a lot of research has gone into it. First of all, yes, it is absolutely true, we do seem disposed to finding distorted human figures and faces particularly distressing. I seem to recall this is also true for other primates as well—that experiments with chimps and bonobos show they react with fear to distorted pictures of chimps and bonobos. It even has a name, the “uncanny valley effect.” Cartoon distortions of human figures look cute to us, but as they get more and more realistic they suddenly hit a point where they become disgusting, frightening, or disturbing. The main hypothesis as far as I know (mind you, this is from my cog sci class in my uni days, so it may be out of date) is disease. Many diseases—end stage syphilis, leprosy, smallpox, and so on—disfigure their victims. People with an aversion to distorted or disfigured people avoided them, so were less likely to die of communicable disease. A predisposition to being afraid of disfigured humans—nearly but not quite human-looking—had positive survival value.

Question: Given rampant car/property crime, why don't police use more tech to help prevent and catch criminals?
Answer: $$$money$$$ Ultimately, the limiting factor in catching criminals is money. Fun fact: You don’t decrease crime by making penalties more severe, you decrease crime by increasing the likelihood of being caught. Which would deter you from speeding more, if the fine for speeding went up by $50, or if the odds of being caught for speeding went up to 98%? Past qa certain point, though, you start getting into cost/benefit questions. It’s not just about police funding, though that’s a part of it—if the police suddenly caught twice as many criminals, you’d now need twice as many judges, twice as many jurors, twice as many courthouses, twice as many lawyers…you get the picture.[1] Society decides what level of crime, and what types of criminal behavior, it’s willing to tolerate because not tolerating it costs too much. Different societies set that level in different places; in the US, we’re willing to tolerate a very high level of property crime that other countries are not, but we are, by the standards of other developed Western nations, absolutely batshit draconian about certain forms of drug offenses—willing to throw ever-increasing, and quite staggering, amounts of money at drug enforcement even as we as a society are quite happy tolerating social ills that increase drug abuse. Go figure. (It’s almost as if there are for-profit industries making money on drug enforcement…oh, wait.) So yeah, the police absolutely could use tech to catch more criminals, especially low-level and midlevel property crime. But that means more money for tech, more money for training to use the tech, more money for police to catch the criminals, more money for courts, for detention, for porbation and parole. We have simply decided it’s not worth it. As the Architect told Neo, “There are levels of survival we are prepared to accept.” [1] Yes, I know it wouldn’t necessarily scale to exactly twice as many, because the bulk of the new criminals would be minor offenders, but you still get the point: increasing the rate at which you catch criminals increases the cost of the entire judicial system, not just law enforcement.

Question: What’s the best way to write simple intriguing single character or two character concept short stories when your brain typically goes towards epic sci-fi?
Answer: Practice. Look, I absolutely get it. Writing short stories is hard. Arguably harder, at least for some of us, than writing novels. Left to my own devices, I seem to land somewhere between 110,000 and 130,000 words in anything I write, except for this absolute beast of a novel my Talespinner and I are working on, which is currently at 107,050 words out of what we’re expecting to be 160,000 or so. Practice. A short story is a very different form. (I recently tried my hand at a simple two-character erotic short for an anthology. No sex appeared until 4,094 words in, and the entire short is 14,442 words in its first draft, which is not how you’re supposed to do erotic short stories. Mark Twain famously said “I didn't have time to write a short letter, so I wrote a long one instead,” and he was right. Brevity is about paring everything down to the innermost essence, and that’s a different skill from storytelling. Like all skills, you learn it by doing. Write a story. You’ll likely overshoot the mark, probably by a lot, even if you come at it with a limited cast of characters and what seems a small, tight, self-contained idea. Re-read it. With every paragraph, ask yourself: Is this necessary? What does this add to the story I’m trying to tell? (If your brain tends to go to big ideas and sweeping worlds, one tool you can use to prune your words is to suggest, in only the most minimal way possible, the world, but leave most of it in shadow. The short story form leaves very little room for worldbuilding except at the periphery.) There are other things you can do as well: short, declarative, active-voice sentences, dialogue that hints at relationships between characters without spelling them out, describing your settings with few but vivid details that suggest the scene without elaboration. All those things, though, are practice. Eunice and I have one published collection of shorts, but we cheated by setting it in a world we’d already explored in three novels, so the worldbuilding was, to large extent, shifted elsewhere. Short stories in the context of an existing world are much, much easier than short stories in a new world, so that might be a way to get some of that practice. Good luck!

Question: Is Banksy's art any good?
Answer: Depends. What do you think art is? Is he technically proficient? I’ve heard people say things like “he just uses stencils,” which, I mean, I get why people confuse technique with art. When I was a kid, I neve understood why the art world likes Picasso. I would look at stuff like this: And I was like “are you serious? A kindergartener could draw this!” Then I saw his early stuff: Picasso did this when he was fifteen. The techniques used in any particular piece of art don’t necessarily tell you anything about the artist’s technical proficiency overall, which leads straight into the next point: Technique is a remarkably poor proxy for artistic merit. Technical proficiency is the mechanical ability to produce what you want to produce. It is not, by itself, the same thing as artistic merit. Thomas Kinkade has, within a certain proscribed realm, technical proficiency. I find his work artistically bankrupt and devoid of meaning. So what exactly does it mean for art to be “good”? If you can’t define what you mean by “good,” basically you’re just arguing semantics. Does Banksy have technical merit? It’s easy to say “nah, he just uses stencils, how hard can it be?” But I think that’s a mistake. His use of space, for example, is extraordinary. I saw this piece in person and it’s brilliant. Everything about the way he uses this found space, even the way she’s facing away from the caption, is brilliant. It also made me cry, which brings up a second definition of “good art,” which is art that makes the audience feel. Banksy does that. Is that enough? No. Art can inspire emotion and still be maudlin or emotionally manipulative. (I don’t think Banksy is, but Kinkade practically defines emotional manipulation.) Which leads into a third part of good art: it represents what the artist intends to represent, it makes the audience feel something, and it has something to say. Judged by that criterion, Banksy is off the charts. Good art is often political. Without that, it risks descending to mere decoration. Most of the great masterpieces are political. Banksy has a lot to say. Like Terry Pratchett, who was an artist in a different medium, you have the sense Banksy is angry, and he turns that anger into biting social commentary. And like Sir Pterry, he is totally okay with using self-referential humor in his repertoire of satiric tools. Is Banksy a good artist? No. By any meaningful measure, he is an outstanding artist.

Question: Why do people say dating sucks if they are in a relationship?
Answer: You know, that’s actually a fascinating question. I’ve heard a lot of people say “dating sucks,” and I’ve asked a lot of people why they think dating sucks, and the answers I get always leave me feeling like I’m talking to some strange alien visitor in a human suit, or perhaps I am a strange alien visitor in a human suit…because man, what they call “dating” and what I call “dating” ain’t on the same planet. Consistently, time after time, year after year, by far the most common answer I get to “why does dating suck?” is: I can’t be myself. I always have to be on my best behavior. I feel like I’m auditioning. And I’m like… Like, I can’t even begin to wrap my head around that. Like, why would you even go into a date from that perspective? Put on a show to try to get your date to like you? The function of a date is to find out if the two of you are compatible and mutually interested in exploring a relationship. Show up with your authentic self, be open without expectation, see if you both come away with the same desire. If you do, awesome! Keep dating. If you don’t, awesome! You’ve learned the two of you aren’t a good match. I’ve had first dates that have gone splendidly. When we met in person, my Talespinner took me to a lovely rum bar where we sat and talked and sipped rum and worked on our novel together, then we had our first kiss beside a fountain. Simple, nothing elaborate, nothing exciting, but it’s one of my all-time favorite first dates ever. I’ve had first dates where I’ve left feeling naah, not gonna work. I’ve had first dates where I’ve left thinking “wow, she’s awesome, I really would like to keep dating her” and she left feeling naah, not gonna work. That’s all okay. Go in open to things working out but not counting on or invested in any particular outcome, and you don’t feel like you’re putting on a show or auditioning or trying to win someone over or whatever. It’s genuinely okay if the answer is no. (I actually think this is related to the difference between an abundance mindset and a starvation mindset of love and connection, and putting on an act because you feel you have to make this date work is one of those self-sabotaging things that leads to dates not working and reinforces a starvation mindset, but that’s a whole conversation outside the scope of this answer.) There’s a bunch of other stuff too: “you need money to date” (you really really don’t, believe me), “dating is a numbers game” (well, maybe if you didn’t think of people as commodities that would change?), “I can’t seem to find anyone who fits into my life” (have you given any thought whatsoever to how you might fit into her life? Any at all?)…but yeah, dating-as-audition? That’s just…I don’t even know what the hell that is.

Question: Which is the best/reliable media to store your data for long term, external HDD/SSD or USB flash drives? Which media has the longest life span?
Answer: Spinning rust HDDs by a country mile. NAND flash memory stores information in electrical charges in tiny devices called “floating gate transistors.” Over time, thanks to Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle, these charges gradually leak out, and the information stored on flash memory, in a literal sense, evaporates. Consumer grade NAND flash SSDs are only guaranteed to store information with the power off for one year. After that, you may start experiencing data corruption and lost files. (This process happens faster at high temperatures; store the SSD above 80F and you might lose data sooner.) Flash memory sticks are even worse. They use the same NAND flash chips with the same floating gate transistors, but they don’t have the sophisticated controllers that do error correction and wear leveling. Conventional spinning hard drives can easily keep data for ten years or more.

Question: Why do we believe that whatever a writer portrays in their work is what they like or believe in?
Answer: Hmm. “Like or believe in” is doing some pretty heavy lifting there. Writer here. I make my living writing novels. The things you’ll find in my novels often are things I like and believe in… …but just as often they’re things that worry or horrify me. My co-author Eunice was at WorldCon with a big pile of our books recently. One of the novels she has with her was immechanica, our near-future, hard-SF dystopia. This is definitely not a world we like and believe in. We extrapolated from real-world tech, political, social, and environmental trends to try to create a worst-case scenario. Our goal was to write a warning, something we feared, not something we liked. And a really fucked-up thing happened at WorldCon. So there’s a passage in immechanica that goes like this: Safan slid a small black case across the table to her. It reminded Nadine a bit of something an engagement ring might come in, about the same width but three times longer. She snapped it open. Inside lay a thing like a mechanical wasp, smooth glossy black, with thin wings of some clear plastic. The front was pointed, with two lenses that suggested eyes. Overall, it had a sleek, menacing look that made Nadine’s skin crawl. “What is it?” “Swarm drone. A bunch of these will follow you in, all controlled remotely. Anyone turns up to give you grief, well…” A nasty grin crossed his face. “You designate a threat. The swarm picks the closest drone, it locks on, fires a propulsive charge, tears into the target and then explodes. Core is a foot of grooved tungsten wire dipped in wax impregnated with quick-acting nerve agent, wrapped around half a gram of crystallized high explosive.” “Jesus.” Nadine dropped the case on the table. “Who comes up with shit like this?” Someone stopped by the Luminastra Press booth at the con to say “yeah, my company is working on explosive micro-drone weapons, how did you know?” When she told me, I was like “Jesus Christ on a tap-dancing camel, immechanica was supposed to be a warning, not a goddamn how-to guide!” Fuck me dead, we weren’t dark enough. So yeah, if you read immechanica and come away with “oh, look, this is what these authors like and believe in,” either we have failed in our role as writers or you need psychiatric help immediately. Now, that said, yes, a lot of our novels do describe things we like and believe in. The Passionate Pantheon novels, set in a far-future, post-scarcity society with virtually limitless radical longevity and strong AI, describe a place we would both like to live. The novels are written as pornography, so of course there’s tons and tons and oodles and tons of really kinky, highly explicit sex…but we use the sex to explore philosophy, meaning, community, accountability, and a bunch of other things we both care passionately about. We also explore ways a utopian post-scarcity society can go wrong. The odd-numbered novels in the series are upbeat utopias; the even-numbered novels are erotic horror, where we take the themes in the odd-numbered books and invert them. We even have a blog where we talk about the philosophical themes in the novels, though we haven’t had time to update it since Eunice started working on her postgraduate degree. So is that a series where we talk about things we like and believe in? Yes, but we also talk about ways it can become problematic, too.

Song lyrics are copyrighted, and the ‘fair use’ exception to copyright infringement for song lyrics is especially narrow. If you don’t have an ASCAP license, yeah, you’re gonna get dinged. “BUT FAIR USE!!!!!!!!!!!” Okay, listen. “Fair use” is a legal affirmative defense you can use in court. If you get sued for copyright infringement, and the case goes to court, “fair use” gives you what is called an “affirmative defense.” An affirmative defense means that you confess to all the elements of the allegation—you tell the prosecutor or plaintiff ‘yes, everything you just said is true and correct, and I admit I did what I am accused of doing’—but then you explain to the court why what you did, which you have admitted to doing, is permissible. “Fair use” is not something that is determined before you go to court. “Fair use” is an argument you make in court AFTER you have been sued and AFTER you have admitted to doing the thing the person who sued you accuses you of doing, but BEFORE the court rules against you.

Question: How can you imply that your narrator is unreliable without leaving their point of view?
Answer: A2A: I like the way Iain Banks did this in Transition. The very first sentence of the novel Transition is “Apparently I am what is known as an Unreliable Narrator, though of course if you believe everything you’re told, you deserve whatever you get.” But assuming you don’t have literary balls you need to lug about in a wheelbarrow: Generally, you show that a narrator is unreliable either directly, by having the narrator relate things in the book that are contradicted by other things in the book, or indirectly, by having him present things from so far within his own experience that the reader says “wha—?” To put it another way, you can show a narrator who is unreliable either in story, by having the narrator lie to other characters, contradict himself, or contradict things he’s stated earlier through his actions, or out of story, by having a narrator who behaves in ways or believes things that the reader finds difficult to believe or unacceptable, even though the narrator appears to sincerely believe his own bullshit. The protagonist from Lolita is a classic example of the second sort. Humbert Humbert clearly believes that what he’s doing is proper and right, and Lolita is driving the action, but a reader approaching the situation from the outside sees him as a predator. There’s also the unreliable narrator who is unreliable because he’s insane. Edgar Allen Poe is a master of this. The narrator is sincere and is not trying to deceive the reader, he’s just nucking futs, and it’s clear to the reader (or should be clear to the reader) that the narration is the product of a disordered mind.

Question: If someone bought Facebook for the purpose of shutting it down, would that be possible?
Answer: Would it be possible to shut down Facebook? Yes, of course. It wouldn’t even be hard, from a technical perspective. Null-route some IP addresses and bam. Would it be possible to buy Facebook? As I type this, Facebook’s market cap is $1,340,000,000,000. Nobody has that much money. Plus as soon as someone started buying Facebook stock, the price would go up. And of course not all Facebook stock is for sale. So no, somebody can’t “buy Facebook.” Even Elon Musk’s wealth is a few orders of magnitude short. You’d need 50 or 60 Elon Musks all burning every penny they had to do it. But wait! You don’t need to buy all the stock, just 50% of it and a bit, right? Well, sure, in theory. Then you could vote in a Board of Directors on-board with your “shut down Facebook” plan, right? Well…maybe, but probably not. Even a majority stakeholder in a publicly traded company can’t shut down the company with a snap of the fingers. The company’s bylaws and the needs of the other stakeholders prevent that. But wait, there’s more! Facebook has different classes of stock with different voting rights. Mark Zuckerberg owns a bit more than 13% of Facebook’s stock. However, he owns about 958,000 shares of Class A and 346.05 million shares of Class B stock as of February 2024, giving him over 61% voting power. So even if you were to buy all of the stock not owned by Zuckerberg, you’d still have only 39% voting shares. So no. You will have spent a little over $1,026,000,000,000 for nothing.
